APL synapses project · step-by-step reports · Report 07 · 2026-11-04

The model pinned to the recordings, and the comparison

QuestionWhen the block model is pinned to the recordings, how well does it predict which odor pairs become more similar when APL is blocked, and does APL's specific wiring improve that prediction?
Inputs
  • The model of Report 05 (hemibrain R, male CNS L and R; corrected calyx, new claws, new ORN table)
  • The recordings and the quantities of Report 06
Outputs
  • with_outside_ROI_synapses/claws_v2m2/odor_weighted/: TNT_vs_model_fits.csv, TNT_vs_model_nulls.csv, TNT_vs_model_odor_pairs.csv, TNT_vs_model_per_odor.csv, TNT_vs_model_summary.json, TNT_vs_model.png
Scripts

  • scripts/reports/r07_model_vs_tnt.py (this report)

Report 05 ran the model with assumed coding levels (20% of KCs respond with APL blocked, 10% intact). Here the model is instead pinned to the recordings: the fraction of KCs responding to each odor with APL blocked is set to the TNT fraction for that odor, and the mean intact fraction to TNT3c's. The model's change in similarity is then compared with the data's, pair by pair. The pinning sets coding levels only. The pattern of similarity changes across pairs is not fitted, so it is a prediction.

What changed in this revision (2026-11-04)

The model is rebuilt on the corrected calyx, the new claws and the new ORN table; version MC (per-KC counts plus bouton inhibition per glomerulus) is added.

Equation 1 (the input gain gog_ogo​) is worked through with a mock example.

New: why the ratio to the ceiling is squared, with a simulation.

The suppression figure has a y = x line and equal axes.

1Step 1: pinning each odor to the TNT fraction

With APL blocked the model is yko=[xko−θ]+y_{ko} = [x_{ko} - \theta]_+yko​=[xko​−θ]+​. Instead of one threshold for all odors, each odor's glomerular responses are multiplied by a gain gog_ogo​, with θ=1\theta = 1θ=1. The gain is chosen so that exactly the TNT fraction of KCs exceeds the threshold:

xko=go∑gWkg rgo,go=θQo ⁣(1−ϕoTNT)(1)x_{ko} = g_o \sum_g W_{kg}\, r_{go}, \qquad g_o = \frac{\theta}{Q_o\!\left(1 - \phi^{\mathrm{TNT}}_o\right)} \tag{1}xko​=go​g∑​Wkg​rgo​,go​=Qo​(1−ϕoTNT​)θ​(1)
Qo(q)Q_o(q)Qo​(q) = the qqq-quantile over KCs of ∑gWkgrgo\sum_g W_{kg} r_{go}∑g​Wkg​rgo​; dividing by it puts the KC at that quantile exactly at threshold

So an odor that drives 25% of units in TNT drives 25% of model KCs with APL blocked. Only the order of the KCs' drives comes from the connectome and the ORN (or GH146) responses; the level comes from the data. Then, with APL intact, a single APL gain aaa per mushroom body and version is calibrated so that the mean fraction over odors equals TNT3c's (6.83% for the 16 odors). How much each odor is suppressed is left to the model.

1.1Equation 1 with numbers: a mock example

The goal of pinning is that, with APL blocked, the model drives exactly the fraction of KCs that TNT drives for each odor. The threshold is fixed at θ = 1, and each odor's input is multiplied by a gain gog_ogo​ chosen so that the right number of KCs end up above 1. Here is the calculation for a mock mushroom body of 10 KCs and one odor that drives 20% of units in TNT:

  • 1. Unscaled drives ∑gWkgrgo\sum_g W_{kg} r_{go}∑g​Wkg​rgo​ of the 10 KCs: 0.12, 0.30, 0.05, 0.42, 0.22, 0.18, 0.60, 0.35, 0.08, 0.50.
  • 2. Sort them: 0.05, 0.08, 0.12, 0.18, 0.22, 0.30, 0.35, 0.42, 0.50, 0.60.
  • 3. The quantile. 20% should respond, so the threshold must sit at the 80th percentile, Qo(1−0.20)=Qo(0.80)Q_o(1 - 0.20) = Q_o(0.80)Qo​(1−0.20)=Qo​(0.80). With 10 values its position is 0.80 × 9 = 7.2 places from the bottom (counting from 0): between the 8th value (0.42) and the 9th (0.50), 20% of the way: 0.42 + 0.2 × (0.50 − 0.42) = 0.436.
  • 4. The gain. go=θ/Qo(0.80)=1/0.436g_o = \theta / Q_o(0.80) = 1 / 0.436go​=θ/Qo​(0.80)=1/0.436 = 2.294.
  • 5. Scaled drives xko=go∑gWkgrgox_{ko} = g_o \sum_g W_{kg} r_{go}xko​=go​∑g​Wkg​rgo​: 0.28, 0.69, 0.11, 0.96, 0.50, 0.41, 1.38, 0.80, 0.18, 1.15. Exactly two (from 0.60 and 0.50) are above 1, so 2 of 10 = 20% respond, as in TNT. The KC at 0.42 ends just below, at 0.96.

Dividing by the quantile only moves the threshold to the right place in each odor's distribution. The order of the KCs' drives (which KC responds) still comes from the connectome and the ORN responses. An odor with weak ORN responses has small drives, a small quantile, and therefore a large gain (Figure 1b).

2Step 2: the APL versions compared

All versions of Report 05 are run with the same pinning, plus two in which APL's activity is fed forward from the PNs instead of fed back from the KCs:

F0: yko=[xko−1−a Aoff]+,Aoff=∑gwg gorgo∑gwg;F: the same with wg replaced by wg p~g in(2)\text{F0: } y_{ko} = \left[x_{ko} - 1 - a\,A^{\mathrm{ff}}_o\right]_+, \quad A^{\mathrm{ff}}_o = \frac{\sum_g w_g\, g_o r_{go}}{\sum_g w_g}; \qquad \text{F: the same with } w_g \text{ replaced by } w_g\,\tilde p^{\,\mathrm{in}}_g \tag{2}F0: yko​=[xko​−1−aAoff​]+​,Aoff​=∑g​wg​∑g​wg​go​rgo​​;F: the same with wg​ replaced by wg​p~​gin​(2)

In F0, APL's activity is the odor's mean KC input, so it does not depend on how many KCs respond. In F, glomeruli with more PN→APL synapses contribute more to it.

3Step 3: how model and data are compared

  • Odor-pair pattern, rrr: the Pearson correlation over odor pairs between ΔSabdata\Delta S^{\mathrm{data}}_{ab}ΔSabdata​ and ΔSabmodel\Delta S^{\mathrm{model}}_{ab}ΔSabmodel​. The model value is averaged over the three mushroom bodies before the correlation. Every pair counts (120 with ORN input, 78 with GH146).
  • Odor-label permutation ppp: the odor labels of the model matrix are permuted 5,000 times. This keeps the matrix structure and tests whether the match depends on which odor is which.
  • Bootstrap range: recordings are resampled with replacement within each condition (2,000 draws), and the 5th–95th percentile of rrr is reported.
  • Wiring nulls: each wiring version is re-solved with its wiring shuffled 200 times per mushroom body. C swaps (uk,vk)(u_k, v_k)(uk​,vk​) pairs among KCs of the same class. P and M shuffle pgp_gpg​ across glomeruli. F shuffles p~gin\tilde p^{\mathrm{in}}_gp~​gin​. ppp is the share of shuffles with rrr at least as high as the real wiring.
  • Ceiling: because the data are noisy, even a perfect model would not reach r=1r = 1r=1. The split-half reliability of ΔSdata\Delta S^{\mathrm{data}}ΔSdata (Spearman–Brown corrected) is 0.70, which caps rrr near 0.70\sqrt{0.70}0.70​ = 0.84 (explained in Section 4).
  • Suppression: Spearman ρ\rhoρ over odors between data and model sos_oso​.

4Results

With uniform APL, rrr = 0.49 with ORN input (permutation ppp = 0.001; bootstrap 0.28–0.53) and 0.41 with GH146 input. Against the ceiling of 0.84, that is about (0.49/0.84)2≈(0.49/0.84)^2 \approx(0.49/0.84)2≈ 35% of the reproducible pattern (why squared: below). Per mushroom body rrr is 0.39 (hemibrain R), 0.56 (male CNS L), 0.45 (male CNS R).

4.1Why the ratio to the ceiling is squared

A correlation r is not a share. Its square, r2r^2r2, is: the share of the data's variance that the model accounts for. The reasoning goes in three steps.

  • The data are part pattern, part noise. The split-half reliability of ΔS\Delta SΔS is 0.702: 70% of its variance over pairs is reproducible pattern, and 30% is recording noise that changes from one set of recordings to the next.
  • A perfect model can explain only the pattern. Its r2r^2r2 would be 0.702, so its r would be 0.702\sqrt{0.702}0.702​ = 0.838. That is the ceiling.
  • The uniform model. r = 0.49, so r2r^2r2 = 0.244: it accounts for 24% of all the variance, which is 35% of the 70% that is pattern. That is r2/reliability=(r/ceiling)2r^2 / \text{reliability} = (r / \text{ceiling})^2r2/reliability=(r/ceiling)2.

A quick simulation confirms it: 120 mock pairs whose "data" are 70% pattern and 30% noise, and a mock model that shares 35% of its variance with the pattern. The model correlates with the noisy data at r = 0.49 on average and with the noise-free pattern at r = 0.58 (0.5920.59^20.592 = 0.35). The unsquared ratio 0.49/0.84 = 0.59 is that second correlation; squaring turns it into a share.

  • Feedback matters. Uniform feedback gives r = 0.49; inhibition fed forward from the PNs (F0, F) gives r = 0.42 and 0.45. Report 08 explains why.
  • Specific wiring. The wiring versions (C, P0, P, M0, M, MC) change rrr from U's by −0.02 to −0.00 with ORN input, and −0.02 to +0.04 with GH146. Against their own shuffles, C with GH146 input (ppp = 0.015, r = 0.45) passes at ppp < 0.05; every other test does not. L (inhibition on claws per glomerulus) gives r = 0.37 (ORN) and 0.33 (GH146).
  • Suppression per odor is not predicted (ρ ≤ 0.35).
  • Size. The model's mean change (+0.078) is 0.44 times the data's (+0.178).
Caveats

Inputs are ORN or GH146 averages from other flies, not the recorded flies' PNs. Imaged units are not identified KCs.

Three mushroom bodies from two connectomes. Their uniform-model fits range from 0.39 to 0.56 (ORN input), so wiring tests that average over them have little power.

Many tests: of 8 real-vs-shuffle tests on odor pairs, one passes at ppp < 0.05: C with GH146 input (ppp = 0.015, r = 0.45). With 8 tests, about 0.4 would pass by chance alone.
